name: Pechenegs
info: The Pechenegs were a semi-nomadic Turkic people from Central Asia who controlled much of the steppes of southeast Europe and the Crimean Peninsula in the 9th and 10th centuries, raiding Kievan Rus' and serving Byzantium.

facts.capital: None known: a nomadic realm, Patzinakia, divided into eight provinces
facts.predecessor: Pecheneg groups between the Aral Sea and the Syr Darya, descended from the Kangars according to Omeljan Pritsak
facts.successor: The Cumans and Torks on the Pontic steppe; Pecheneg settlers in the Byzantine Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary

t: Driven west by the Oghuz, the Khazars and the Cumans, the Pechenegs drove the Magyars west of the Dnieper by 892, pushing them towards Pannonia, where the Magyars later founded the Hungarian state.
For more than two centuries they raided the lands of Rus'; in 972 they ambushed and killed Sviatoslav I of Kiev, and in 1036 Yaroslav I the Wise defeated them.
A combined Byzantine and Cuman army under Alexios I Komnenos annihilated them as an independent force at the Battle of Levounion in 1091.
dyk: According to the Primary Chronicle, the Pecheneg Khan Kurya made a chalice from the skull of Sviatoslav I of Kiev, in accordance with the custom of steppe nomads.

sections.foundation:
The Pechenegs, called Patzinakoi by Byzantine writers and Bjnak or Bajanak in Arabic and Persian texts, were a semi-nomadic Turkic people who spoke the Pecheneg language. According to Omeljan Pritsak their homeland lay between the Aral Sea and the middle course of the Syr Darya, on trade routes linking Central Asia with Eastern Europe, and they descended from the Kangars, listed among the subject peoples of the Eastern Turkic Khaganate. Victor Spinei holds that the first certain reference to them is an 8th-century Uyghur envoy's report, surviving in Tibetan, of fighting between the Be-ča-nag and the Hor near the Syr Darya.

After the Turkic Khaganate collapsed in 744, the Oghuz moved west against them. Al-Masudi records that the Oghuz, Karluks and Kimaks defeated the Pechenegs near the Aral Sea before 850; most then migrated towards the Volga and settled between the Ural and Volga rivers, while some joined the Oghuz. Attacked from two sides by the Khazars and the Oghuz, they moved west again across the Khazar Khaganate and expelled the Hungarians from the Kuban and the upper Donets. Pritsak dates this second migration to around 830, but Kristó suggests it could hardly have happened before the 850s.
sections.socioeconomy:
Muslim writers drawing on 9th-century sources describe the Pecheneg territory between the Ural and Volga as a thirty-day walk across, bordered by the Cumans, Khazars, Oghuz Turks and Slavs. The Pechenegs raided their neighbours regularly, especially the Khazars and their vassals the Burtas, and sold their captives into slavery. Their 8th-century wars with the Oghuz were most probably fought for control of trade routes, and when the Uzes later expelled them from their homeland they seized most of their livestock and other goods.

Their language, which died out centuries ago, is known mainly from the names of their provinces recorded by Constantine Porphyrogenitus. Mahmud al-Kashgari thought it a variant of the Cuman and Oghuz idioms, and Anna Komnene said the Pechenegs and Cumans shared a common language. Scholars have placed it in the Oghuz or the Kipchak branch of the Turkic family, though it is too poorly documented to classify with certainty. Pecheneg communities later settled widely: around 150 villages in the Kingdom of Hungary, and places from Romania to Poland and Turkey still bear their name.
sections.military:
The Pechenegs fought every neighbour in turn: the Byzantine Empire, Bulgaria, Kievan Rus', Khazaria and the Magyars. Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria employed them against the Magyars, and after the Battle of Southern Buh they drove the Magyars out of Etelköz and the Pontic steppes. From the 9th century they raided the lands of Rus' for more than two centuries, sometimes in full-scale wars such as Igor of Kiev's war on them in 920; at other times they allied with the Rus', as on Igor's Byzantine campaign of 943.

In 968 they besieged Kiev. Some joined Sviatoslav I in his Byzantine campaign of 970–971, but in 972 they ambushed and killed him. The fortunes of the war swung under Vladimir I of Kiev, who founded the town of Pereyaslav on the site of his victory over them, and Yaroslav I the Wise defeated them in 1036. Pecheneg mercenaries served under the Byzantines at the Battle of Manzikert. A combined Byzantine and Cuman army under Alexios I Komnenos annihilated them as an independent force at the Battle of Levounion in 1091, and the Byzantines defeated them again at the Battle of Beroia in 1122, on the territory of present-day Bulgaria.
sections.governance:
Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, writing about 950, described Patzinakia as stretching west to the Siret River and divided into eight provinces under the same number of great princes, four tribes on each side of the Dnieper, reflecting the Turkic division into left and right. The eight tribes were divided in turn into 40 sub-tribes, probably clans. He named the provinces Irtim, Tzour, Gyla, Koulpeï, Charaboï, Talmat, Chopon and Tzopon, and the princes who led them when they were expelled from their earlier lands. Peter Golden, following Németh and Ligeti, proposes that each tribal name joined an equine coat colour to the ruler's title.

Three of the tribes, the Erdim, Čur and Yula, formed the Kangars, deemed “more valiant and noble than the rest”. The late 10th-century Hudud al-'Alam distinguished the “Turkic Pechenegs” of the Donets from the “Khazarian Pechenegs” of the Kuban, probably those who accepted Khazar suzerainty. Later leaders known by name include Kurya in the 970s, Metiga in the 980s and Kuchug in the 990s. Their statecraft has been judged to have gone little beyond attacks on neighbours and spells as mercenaries for other powers.
sections.impact:
The Pechenegs helped redraw the map of eastern Europe. By 892 they had driven the Magyars west of the Dnieper, and their pressure made the Magyars leave Etelköz forever and settle in Pannonia, where they later founded the Hungarian state. In the 9th century Byzantium allied with them to fend off Kievan Rus' and the Magyars. Their wars against Kievan Rus' led the Slavs of the Walachian lands to migrate north of the Dniestr in the 10th and 11th centuries. Byzantine emperors used Pecheneg troops again and again, from the Battle of Manzikert to the wars in southern Italy.

Their remnants spread across the Balkans and Hungary. One of the earliest introductions of Islam into Eastern Europe came through an early 11th-century Muslim prisoner of the Byzantines who was brought among the Pechenegs and converted some of them, and in the late 12th century Abu Hamid al-Gharnati wrote of Hungarian Pechenegs, probably Muslims, living disguised as Christians. In Hungary the title of Comes Bissenorum, Count of the Pechenegs, lasted for centuries, and some historians believe that Pechenegs contributed to the origins of the Karakalpaks.
sections.decline:
After their defeat in 1036 the weakened Pechenegs were replaced on the Pontic steppe by the Cumans and the Torks; Mykhailo Hrushevsky wrote that the horde moved to the Danube, crossed it and disappeared from the Pontic steppes. After the Battle of Levounion in 1091 Alexios I recruited the defeated Pechenegs and settled them in the district of Moglena as a tagma of the Moglena Pechenegs. The Cumans attacked them again in 1094, and many Pechenegs were slain or absorbed.

Pecheneg troops still fought for Byzantium: at Otranto in 1105 or 1106 against Bohemond, and for Manuel I Komnenos in southern Italy against William the Bad, some of them at the Battle of Andria in 1155. The Pechenegs as a group were last mentioned in 1168, among the Chorni Klobuky, the “Black Hats”. Those south of the Danube were assimilated, mostly with Romanians and Bulgarians. The Pechenegs of Hungary were probably decimated by the Mongol invasion, but names of Pecheneg origin went on appearing in documents, and in 15th-century Tolna county some people took the surname Besenyő. The village of Pečenjevce in southeast Serbia was founded by Pechenegs who found refuge there after the war with Byzantium.

summary: The Pechenegs were a semi-nomadic Turkic people who left Central Asia in the 9th century and dominated the steppes north of the Black Sea and the Crimea. They drove the Magyars west, served and fought Byzantium, Bulgaria and Kievan Rus', and were broken at the Battle of Levounion in 1091, after which their remnants were absorbed by their neighbours.
references: Florin Curta, Southeastern Europe in the Middle Ages, 500-1250 (Cambridge University Press, 2006)
Peter B. Golden, An Introduction to the History of the Turkic People (Otto Harrassowitz, 1992)
C. A. Macartney, The Magyars in the Ninth Century (Cambridge University Press, 1968)

Victor Spinei, The Great Migrations in the East and South East of Europe from the Ninth to the Thirteenth Century (Romanian Cultural Institute, 2003)
Victor Spinei, The Romanians and the Turkic Nomads North of the Danube Delta from the Tenth to the Mid-Thirteenth century (Brill, 2009)

pointDescs.860: Defeated near the Aral Sea before 850 and attacked by the Khazars and the Oghuz, the Pechenegs have moved west and settled along the Donets and the Kuban.
pointDescs.889: Driven further west by the Khazars and Cumans, the Pechenegs advance into the steppes north of the Black Sea.
pointDescs.892: The Pechenegs drive the Magyars west of the Dnieper and soon out of Etelköz and the Pontic steppes.
pointDescs.920: Igor of Kiev wages war on the Pechenegs, one of the many wars and raids between them and the Rus'.
pointDescs.950: Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus describes Patzinakia, reaching west to the Siret River and divided into eight provinces under eight great princes.
pointDescs.968: The Pechenegs, masters of much of the steppes of southeast Europe and the Crimea, besiege Kiev.
pointDescs.972: The Pechenegs ambush and kill Sviatoslav I of Kiev; Khan Kurya is said to have made a chalice from his skull.
pointDescs.990: Under Vladimir I of Kiev the fortunes of the Rus'-Pecheneg wars swing, and he founds Pereyaslav on the site of a victory over them.
pointDescs.1036: Yaroslav I the Wise defeats the Pechenegs, and the Cumans and Torks soon replace them on the Pontic steppe.
pointDescs.1091: A Byzantine and Cuman army under Alexios I Komnenos annihilates the Pechenegs as an independent force at the Battle of Levounion.

notes: The register's start year 860 is not an event the article dates; the first point describes the situation after the migrations (before 850; the second migration c. 830 or after the 850s).
Vladimir I's reign is given in the article as 990-995, which is not his usual dating; I used 990 for his victory without a firmer year.
The Battle of Manzikert is undated in the article, so it is not used as a point or event.
The judgement that Pecheneg statecraft went no further than raids and mercenary service is the article's own unattributed view; written as 'has been judged'.
Language classification: the article says both 'thought to have belonged to the Oghuz branch' and 'most probably Kipchak (Németh, Ligeti) or Oguz (Baskakov)'; written as Oghuz or Kipchak.
